opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most underrated things, especially in a field like mechanistic interpretability, which is very empirical. So much of research is just running experiments, looking at the results, forming a hypothesis, and running more experiments, and the speed of that feedback loop is a massive determinant of how productive you are. If it takes you a day to test an idea, you'll test maybe a handful of ideas a week. If it takes you twenty minutes, you can test dozens, and you build intuitions much faster because you're getting contact with reality so much more often.

Coding skill isn't really about being able to write beautiful, production-quality software. Research code is often hacky and throwaway, and I think people coming from software engineering sometimes over-engineer things. The useful skill is more like: can you go from "I wonder if this is true" to an actual answer as quickly and reliably as possible? That means being fluent with your tools, knowing your libraries well enough that you're not constantly looking things up, being able to whip up a quick visualization, and, crucially, being good at noticing and debugging bugs. In ML especially, bugs are often silent. Your code runs, it gives you a number, and the number is wrong, and you can end up building an entire narrative on top of an artifact. So a lot of good research engineering is a kind of paranoia: sanity checks, looking at your data, checking that things behave as expected on simple cases.

There's also a lower-friction effect that's easy to underrate. If running an experiment feels effortful, you subconsciously avoid doing it, and you spend more time theorizing in your head, which in my experience is usually much less productive than just looking. When coding feels cheap, you're much more willing to try the slightly weird idea or check the thing you're 90% sure about, and that's often where the interesting results come from.

And it compounds. Good infrastructure, good habits, and reusable tooling mean every future experiment gets faster. These days, AI coding assistants change the picture somewhat, since they handle a lot of the boilerplate, but I think they amplify good judgment rather than replace it. You still need to know what you want, structure the problem well, and catch when the output is subtly wrong. So I'd say coding is less a separate skill from research and more the medium through which you actually do empirical research. Being good at it is just being able to think faster in that medium.

r001.rationale: The response says research code is often hacky and throwaway, and that production-quality software is not the useful standard.

r002.rationale: It identifies the speed of the experiment feedback loop as a massive determinant of research productivity.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a few things going on here. The most obvious one is just speed. In empirical research, and especially in something like interpretability, the bottleneck is very often the iteration loop: you have a question, you write some code to test it, you look at the result, you go "huh, that's weird," and you form a new question. If each cycle of that loop takes you an hour, you get maybe five or six experiments in a day. If it takes you five minutes, you get dozens. And the compounding effect of that is enormous, because research is fundamentally about being confused and gradually becoming less confused, and each experiment is a chance to update.

The second thing, which I think people underrate, is that being a strong coder changes which experiments you're even willing to try. If writing the code feels painful, you'll unconsciously shy away from the messy, fiddly experiments, and you'll gravitate towards the ones that are easy to implement. But the easy-to-implement experiments are often not the most informative ones. Someone who's fluent will just go "oh, I'll quickly hack together a thing that caches the activations and patches them in at layer twelve," and they'll do it in twenty minutes and learn something. Someone who isn't fluent will think about it, decide it sounds like a lot of work, and not do it. So fluency expands the space of ideas you'll actually act on.

The third thing is debugging, which I'd say is maybe the most underrated research skill in general. A huge fraction of research is things not working, and it's often really unclear whether that's because your hypothesis is wrong or because you have a bug. And being good at coding means being good at quickly ruling out the bug explanation, writing sanity checks, visualising intermediate results, that sort of thing. I've seen people spend weeks chasing a "finding" that turned out to be an off-by-one error in how they indexed the tokens. The researchers I know who are really productive tend to have a very strong instinct for "wait, that number looks suspicious, let me check it" before they get excited.

I'd add a caveat, which is that it's not about being a great software engineer in the traditional sense. Research code is throwaway code most of the time. You don't need beautiful abstractions or tests for everything. What you want is to be fast and to be correct, and those are somewhat different skills from building a production system. In fact, I think some people coming from a software engineering background slow themselves down by over-engineering things. The ideal is kind of a Jupyter notebook mindset: hack it together, look at it, throw most of it away, and only clean up the bits that turn out to be load-bearing.

And honestly, this is one of the things where I think people should just practice a lot. Pick a paper, try to reproduce the core result in a day, and notice where you get stuck. That tends to be really informative about what skills you're actually missing.

r001.rationale: The response says research code is usually throwaway, recommends hacking things together in a Jupyter notebook, and says production-style engineering is unnecessary.

r002.rationale: It identifies the speed of the research iteration loop as a major factor, explaining that faster cycles allow more experiments and compound into greater productivity.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of it is about shortening the loop between having an idea and finding out whether it’s any good. You have some hypothesis about what a model is doing, and you want to run an experiment, look at the results, notice something weird, and try a follow-up. If each of those steps takes you a day of fighting with your code, it’s much harder to make progress.

And I think this matters for your thinking, too. If an experiment feels cheap, you’re much more willing to try a speculative idea. If it feels expensive, you can spend ages trying to reason out whether it’ll work, when actually you could just check.

There’s also a correctness component. Getting a graph out is not the same as having tested your hypothesis. You need to be able to understand what your code is doing, catch bugs, and put in sanity checks. Otherwise you can spend a surprisingly long time explaining an interesting result that turns out to be a broadcasting error.

So the useful skill is being able to turn a research question into a quick, reliable experiment. Writing elegant code can help with that, but the research question is what should be driving it.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes quick, reliable experiments but does not say that small-scale or hacky coding is sufficient for research.

r002.rationale: It identifies shortening the idea-to-experiment loop and making follow-up experiments cheap as key to making research progress.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of it is about shortening the loop between having an idea and finding out whether it’s true. In mechanistic interpretability, you might have a hypothesis about what a model is doing, but then you need to get the relevant activations, run an intervention, plot the results, and check that your code actually measures what you think it measures. If each of those steps is painful, you get to try far fewer ideas.

And there’s a related thing where, if coding takes all of your attention, it’s hard to keep thinking about the research question. Being fluent enough that the implementation is fairly automatic leaves you more room to notice, ‘Hang on, this result is weird,’ or, ‘Actually, there’s a much simpler experiment I could do.’

I wouldn’t equate that with knowing lots of programming languages or being amazing at interview problems. It’s more about being able to turn a fuzzy question into a reliable experiment quickly, and being good enough at debugging that you don’t spend a week interpreting a bug as an exciting discovery.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes coding fluency and reliable experiments, but does not say that small-scale, hacky coding is often sufficient for research.

r002.rationale: It describes shortening the loop from idea to evidence and says painful steps mean trying far fewer ideas, identifying rapid iteration as a major productivity benefit.
